newsitem.title: USA: After visit by China critics, U.S. hosts Qian.
newsitem.headline: After visit by China critics, U.S. hosts Qian.

text.p: After hosting two prominent critics of Beijing, the United States this week turns its attention to Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

The Washington visit begins with Qian spending most of Monday in meetings with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Qian is also to meet President Bill Clinton before leaving Washington on Wednesday.

Talks are expected to focus on Hong Kong, arms sales, human rights and proposed Korean peninsula peace talks, although trade and political donations to American election campaigns also will come up, U.S. officials say.

The visit is aimed at making progress toward a summit later this year between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin and at promoting a bilateral effort to improve still prickly relations through increased exchange visits and cooperation.

U.S. officials predict no dramatic breakthroughs in the Qian talks but stress the need to make progress on major areas of concern, like weapons proliferation, so as to ensure the summit has concrete achievements, not just rhetoric.
Among the summit goals is to get to a point where Clinton could authorize implementation of a 1985 Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation agreement that would give Beijing access to advanced U.S. technology.

But to do that, China would have to greatly improve export controls, among other steps. U.S. officials say Beijing has done little toward this goal, part of a 1996 commitment, but it is still conceiveable China could take sufficient action by the summit to warrant implementing the PNC accord.

Qian flies to New York on Sunday and then to Washington on Monday morning. He arrives one week after Martin Lee, Hong Kong's leading pro-democracy activist, and the Dalai Lama, Tibet's spiritual leader and an advocate for Tibetan autonomy from Beijing, pressed their cases in the U.S. capital.

China was displeased that both leaders were received by Clinton and Albright but its reaction was muted. U.S. officials said this reflected a confidence based on Jiang's successful visit to Moscow and Beijing's defeat of a critical resolution at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
Qian last met Albright on her Feb. 24 trip to China. Since then, Vice President Al Gore also visited Beijing, drawing criticism at home for not being tough enough on human rights.

In addition, recent reports that top Chinese officials may have approved attempts to influence U.S. elections has caused a furor here, fueling critics who would like to end U.S. most favored nation trade status for China.
Clinton on Friday tried to bring balance to the controversy, telling reporters that many other nations -- including Israel and Greece -- also try to influence U.S. government policies.

The Washington Post reported on Friday that senior officials in Beijing may have coordiated an alleged campaign to funnel money secretly into last year's presidential and congressional campaigns, an act the newspaper said would be illegal.

Clinton urged no judgment until all the facts are in but restated the administration's position that if such activity were proven it could have serious consequences for U.S.-China ties, which have begun to improve after six difficult years.

Despite this, U.S. officials seem reasonably confident they can persuade Congress to renew Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade benefits for China for one year. Their primary argument now is that withdrawing MFN would be a devastating blow to Hong Kong, just as the British colony reverts to Chinese control on July 1.
Hong Kong will figure prominently in talks with Qian, with Washington pressing Beijing to maintain the colony's civil and political liberties, which critics say are already eroding.

U.S. officials will also urge China to encourage North Korea to enter into four-party peace talks. The effort stalled last week when North Korea tied its participation to more food aid, lifting U.S. sanctions and diplomatic recognition.
